specPoints.text: know and use the relationship between efficiency, useful energy output and total energy output: efficiency = useful energy output ×100% total energy output
describe a variety of everyday and scientific devices and situations, explaining the transfer of the input energy in terms of the above relationship, including their representation by Sankey diagrams

primer.text: Efficiency turns the conservation law into a score: of all the energy leaving a device, how much served the purpose? This note fixes the equation, works a fan motor from 300 J to 72%, and teaches Sankey diagrams — the arrow picture where widths are joules and efficiency is visible at a glance.

lessons.title: Efficiency and the efficiency equation
sourceHeadings: What is efficiency in an energy transfer?
lessons.opening: Efficiency scores an energy transfer: what fraction of the output actually serves the purpose? It is the useful share of the output expressed as a percentage — and conservation of energy pins the total output to the total input, with the wasted share filling the gap.
keyPoints: Efficiency scores how much of a transfer is wasted.
High efficiency means most of the transferred energy is useful; low efficiency means most is wasted.
By conservation of energy, what leaves equals what arrives.
The output splits into the useful share plus the wasted share.

low.restatement: Efficiency is a percentage score: useful output over total output, where the total equals the input by conservation and the wasted share fills whatever the useful share leaves.
low.analogy: A goalkeeper’s save percentage: saves (useful) divided by all shots faced (total output) — the rest conceded (wasted).
low.examPointer: Write the equation with × 100% for a percentage, or without it for a ratio between 0 and 1 — match the form the question asks for.

medium.restatement: The arithmetic chain is fixed: total output = total input (conservation), useful output = total output − wasted, then divide useful by total and scale by 100 for the percentage.
medium.analogy: A pay slip: gross pay (input) arrives, tax and pension (wasted) are deducted, and take-home (useful) divided by gross is the efficiency.
medium.examPointer: Efficiency above 100% is impossible — that claim is a favourite true-or-false check and conservation is the reason.

check.stem: Efficiency is defined as the ratio of:

options.text: wasted energy output to total energy output
options.explanation: That scores the WASTE, not the efficiency.

options.text: useful energy output to total energy output
options.explanation: This is the stated definition of efficiency.

options.text: total energy input to useful energy output
options.explanation: This is the reciprocal of the efficiency ratio.

options.text: useful energy output to total energy input only
options.explanation: The definition uses total output, which equals total input — but the stated ratio is to output.

check.stem: A motor receives 300 J and wastes 85 J. Its useful energy output is:

options.explanation: Adding the waste back inflates the total beyond the input.
Useful output = 300 - 85 = 215 J.
That is the wasted share.
That is the total output, not the useful share.

check.stem: The same motor’s efficiency is:

options.explanation: That is the wasted share’s percentage, not the efficiency.
This halves the useful share incorrectly.
No real motor converts every joule usefully.

check.stem: Why can the useful output of a device never exceed its total output?

options.explanation: Overheating is a symptom, not the law.

options.text: because useful output can never exceed total output, which equals the input by conservation
options.explanation: The useful share is part of a conserved total.
Nothing doubles here.
The limit is a law, not an instrument artefact.

check.stem: A heater transfers all of its output energy into room heating. What does that make its efficiency?

options.explanation: Nothing produces energy from nothing.

options.text: all of its output energy is useful, i.e. ends up heating the room
options.explanation: For a heater, the intended output is heat, so an all-heat output is fully useful.

options.text: it wastes no energy as sound only
options.explanation: The claim is about ALL output, not one pathway.
Input is still required; only the split changes.

check.stem: State the equation for efficiency as a percentage.
check.modelAnswer: Efficiency is the useful output divided by the total output, multiplied by 100.

check.stem: State the relationship between total energy input and total energy output, and the law behind it.
check.modelAnswer: What leaves the device equals what arrives at it, because of the principle of conservation of energy.

check.stem: Explain why efficiency can also be written as a ratio between 0 and 1, and state what a ratio of 0.4 means.
check.modelAnswer: The × 100% only rescales the fraction; dividing useful output by total output is a ratio by construction, so 0.4 means 40% of the output energy is useful and 60% is wasted.

check.stem: A different motor receives 500 J each second and wastes 150 J. Calculate its useful output and its efficiency.

lessons.title: Sankey diagrams
lessons.opening: A Sankey diagram draws an energy transfer as arrows whose widths are proportional to the energy they carry: one flat input arrow entering, the useful output running straight on, and the wasted output bending away. Because energy is conserved, the widths always recombine to the input width.
keyPoints: A Sankey diagram draws an energy transfer as splitting arrows.
The flat left-hand end is the energy arriving at the system.
The straight arrow to the right represents the useful energy output.
The arrows bending away represent the wasted energy.
Arrow width is proportional to the energy transferred, and total energy in equals total energy out.

low.restatement: Read a Sankey left to right: input width in, straight arrow = useful output, bent arrows = wasted output, and the widths always sum back to the input because energy is conserved.
low.analogy: A river delta: the main channel carries the useful flow onward while side channels bleed away — wider channels mean more water, or here, more joules.
low.examPointer: Widths are PROPORTIONAL, not equal — exam questions test whether you read the arrow widths as energy amounts.

medium.restatement: The three parts of the diagram map exactly onto the three quantities of the efficiency equation: input, useful output and wasted output; conservation is the reason the widths close the balance.
medium.analogy: Splitting a pizza on a plate: the whole pizza arrives (input), the slices guests take are useful, the crumbs on the table are wasted — and nothing left the plate unseen.
medium.examPointer: Learn the two splitting-point equations: total in = total out, and total in = useful out + wasted out.

check.stem: What does the width of each arrow in a Sankey diagram represent?

options.text: the direction of the energy transfer
options.explanation: Direction is shown by the arrow shape, not width.

options.text: the amount of energy being transferred
options.explanation: Widths are proportional to the energy transferred.

options.text: the speed of the energy transfer
options.explanation: Sankeys show amounts, not rates of flow speed.
Temperature appears nowhere in a Sankey.

check.stem: Which part of a Sankey diagram represents the useful energy output?

options.explanation: That is the energy input.

options.text: the straight arrow pointing to the right
options.explanation: The straight arrow is the desired, useful output.
Those are the wasted energy.
Labels describe; arrows carry the energy.

check.stem: What does the flat left-hand end of a Sankey diagram represent?

options.explanation: Waste bends away at the split, not at the flat end.

options.text: the energy transferred into the system
options.explanation: The flat end is the input side of the diagram.
The useful output is the straight arrow on the right.
Efficiency is a ratio of widths, not one arrow.

check.stem: On a Sankey diagram, which conservation equation do the arrow widths always satisfy?

options.text: what arrives = useful share + wasted share
options.explanation: The input splits exactly into useful and waste.

options.text: what arrives = useful share - wasted share
options.explanation: Waste adds, not subtracts.
The split need not be equal.

options.text: total energy in = 2 × useful energy out
options.explanation: No such doubling rule exists.

check.stem: A Sankey’s input arrow is 10 mm wide, the useful arrow is 7 mm and the waste arrow is 3 mm. Which reading is correct?

options.explanation: Widths are proportional to energy, so 7 / 10 = 70% useful.
That is the waste share, not the efficiency.
Adding widths is meaningless here.
The widths recombine exactly: 7 + 3 = 10.

check.stem: State what the arrows that bend away from a Sankey diagram represent.
State the two equations a Sankey diagram satisfies at its splitting point.
check.modelAnswer: Input equals output, and the input splits into the useful share plus the wasted share.

check.stem: Explain how a Sankey diagram shows efficiency without any numbers being written on it.
check.modelAnswer: Because arrow widths are proportional to energy, the useful arrow’s share of the total width IS the efficiency: a wide straight arrow against a thin waste arrow shows a high efficiency, and the comparison works visually because conservation guarantees the widths always recombine to the input width.

check.stem: A Sankey’s input arrow is 8 mm wide and its waste arrow is 2 mm. State the useful energy share as a percentage and describe what the useful arrow’s width must be.
check.modelAnswer: The useful share is 75%, and the useful arrow must be 6 mm wide, because widths are proportional and 8 - 2 = 6 mm must close the balance.

lessons.title: Sankey diagrams of light bulbs and the lifting motor
lessons.opening: Two bulbs drawing the same input make the efficiency lesson visible: the modern bulb keeps its straight arrow wide while the filament bulb bleeds most of its width into heat. The lifting-motor diagram then shows the arithmetic every Sankey can be reduced to: waste = input − useful.
keyPoints: A Sankey for a modern efficient bulb looks very different from an old filament bulb’s.
A more efficient bulb has less wasted energy, shown by a smaller downward heat arrow.
The of-record motor Sankey shows 500 J in and 120 J out usefully.
Wasted = total in minus useful out: the motor’s Sankey reads 500 J in and 120 J out usefully, so 380 J is wasted by subtraction.

low.restatement: Same input, different split: the efficient bulb’s Sankey keeps most width in the straight useful arrow, the filament bulb’s bends most of it away as heat; the motor example turns the widths into 380 J wasted and 24% efficient.
low.analogy: Two funnels of the same mouth: the good one pours almost everything into the bottle, the leaky one dribbles most of it down the outside.
low.examPointer: The Sankey arithmetic move: wasted = total energy in − useful energy out (500 − 120 = 380 J in the of-record example).

medium.restatement: Sankey questions end in one of two calculations: read the widths as joules and subtract for waste, or divide useful by total for the percentage; both rest on the widths being proportional.
medium.analogy: Reading a stained-glass window: the pane widths tell the story without a single number, but a ruler converts them to data when asked.
medium.examPointer: Efficiency from a Sankey = useful width ÷ input width × 100; quote the widths in your working.

check.stem: A modern efficient bulb and an old filament bulb draw the same input. On their Sankey diagrams, the efficient bulb has:

options.explanation: Efficient means LESS waste.

options.text: a narrower waste arrow and a wider useful arrow
options.explanation: Higher efficiency shifts width from the waste arrow to the useful arrow.
Both draw the same input.
Real bulbs still waste some energy.

check.stem: A Sankey shows 500 J entering and 120 J leaving usefully. The wasted energy is:

options.explanation: Adding violates conservation; waste is what the input leaves behind.
That is the useful output.
That is the total input.

check.stem: The same lifting motor’s efficiency is:

options.explanation: That is the waste percentage (380/500), not the efficiency.
This halves the useful share incorrectly.
A motor losing 380 J of 500 J is far from perfect.

check.stem: For an old filament bulb, most of the input arrow’s width:

options.explanation: Filament bulbs waste most energy as heat.

options.text: bends away as heat because the bulb wastes most of its energy
options.explanation: The filament bulb’s waste arrow dominates its Sankey.
Glass is not an energy store in this model.
Energy does not flow back up the supply.

check.stem: Which calculation chain converts a Sankey into the device’s efficiency?

options.text: wasted = input + useful, then efficiency = wasted / input
options.explanation: Both steps are wrong: waste subtracts, and efficiency divides useful by total.

options.text: wasted = input − useful, then efficiency = useful / input × 100
options.explanation: Subtract for the waste share, then divide useful by the total input.
That ratios the two wrong quantities.
That is the reciprocal, which exceeds 100%.

check.stem: State which arrow grows wider when a bulb becomes more efficient at the same input.
check.modelAnswer: The straight useful-output arrow grows wider and the downward wasted-heat arrow shrinks.

check.stem: In the lifting-motor Sankey, state the useful output and the total input.
check.modelAnswer: The useful output is 120 J and the total input is 500 J.

check.stem: Explain why the filament bulb’s Sankey and the efficient bulb’s Sankey can both satisfy conservation while looking so different.
check.modelAnswer: Conservation only fixes the TOTAL width: input = useful + waste. The two bulbs split the same total differently — the efficient bulb gives the straight arrow most of the width, the filament bulb gives the waste arrow most — so both diagrams close their balance while telling opposite efficiency stories.

check.stem: A second motor’s Sankey shows 800 J in and its waste arrow represents 560 J. Calculate the useful output and the efficiency.

glossary.definition: The ratio of the useful energy output from a system to its total energy output, usually as a percentage.
The share of the output energy that serves the intended purpose.
The share of the output energy that does not serve the intended purpose.
A diagram of an energy transfer whose arrow widths are proportional to the energy transferred.

workedExample.prompt: The blades of a fan are turned by an electric motor. In one second, 300 J of energy is transferred electrically from the mains supply and 85 J is wasted due to friction and sound. Calculate the efficiency of the motor.
steps: List the known quantities: total energy input = 300 J and total wasted energy = 85 J.
State the equation: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy output × 100%.
By conservation of energy, total energy output = total energy input = 300 J.
Useful energy output = total energy output - wasted energy = 300 - 85 = 215 J.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The efficiency of the motor is 72% (215 J of every 300 J is useful).
